title: Linux Essentials
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one Linux question per grade level

questions.q: You open a terminal and want to know which directory you are currently in. Which command prints your current working directory?
questions.note: pwd (print working directory) outputs the absolute path of the shell's current location. It is the first navigation command students learn.

explain.correct: pwd stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the full absolute path, e.g. /home/student. It is the canonical way to confirm where you are in the filesystem.
wrong: ls lists the contents of a directory — it shows what is inside your current location, not the location itself.
cd (change directory) moves you to a different directory; it does not print anything unless combined with pwd afterward.
mkdir creates a new directory; it does not display your current location.

questions.q: You have a large log file and you only want to see the last 10 lines on screen. Which command does this by default?
questions.note: tail prints the last 10 lines of a file by default. Contrast with head, which prints the first 10 lines. Both accept a -n flag to change the count.

explain.correct: tail outputs the last 10 lines of a file by default (tail -n 10). It is the standard tool for checking the newest entries in log files.
wrong: cat concatenates and prints the entire file to standard output — it does not limit output to the last 10 lines.
head prints the first 10 lines of a file, not the last.
less opens a file in an interactive pager for scrolling; it does not default to showing only the last 10 lines.

questions.q: You want to copy an entire directory called 'project/' and all its contents to a backup location. Which command correctly performs a recursive copy?
questions.note: cp requires the -r (recursive) flag to copy directories and their contents. Without -r, cp refuses to copy a directory and returns an error.

explain.correct: cp -r copies a directory recursively, duplicating the directory tree and all files within it to the destination path.
wrong: cp project/ backup/ without -r will fail with 'omitting directory project/' — cp does not copy directories unless the recursive flag is supplied.
mv project/ backup/ moves (renames) the directory rather than copying it; the original is removed.
mkdir -p backup/ creates the destination directory but the subsequent cp without -r still fails to copy the directory tree.

questions.q: After running ls -l on a file you see the permissions string -rwxr-xr--. What is the octal (numeric) representation of these permissions?
questions.note: rwx = 7, r-x = 5, r-- = 4, so the octal is 754. Calculating each group (owner/group/other) separately is the standard method taught in CTS2165C.

explain.correct: rwx for owner = 4+2+1 = 7; r-x for group = 4+0+1 = 5; r-- for other = 4+0+0 = 4. Combined: 754.
wrong: 764 would represent rwx rw- r-- (other has write, not execute), which does not match the -rwxr-xr-- string shown.
755 would represent rwx r-x r-x (other has execute), but the string shows r-- for other — no execute bit.
744 would represent rwx r-- r-- (group has only read), but the string shows r-x for group — execute bit is set.

questions.q: A student on Ubuntu wants to install the 'nmap' network scanner. Which command installs it AND automatically resolves its dependencies?
questions.note: apt (Advanced Package Tool) is the high-level package manager on Debian/Ubuntu systems. Unlike dpkg, it automatically downloads and installs all required dependencies.

explain.correct: apt install nmap contacts the configured repositories, resolves all dependencies, downloads the required packages, and installs them automatically — no manual dependency handling required.
wrong: dpkg -i installs a local .deb file directly but does NOT resolve dependencies automatically; missing dependencies must be installed separately.
rpm -i is the Red Hat/Fedora low-level package installer (not used on Ubuntu/Debian) and also does not resolve dependencies automatically.
tar -xzf extracts a compressed archive; it is not a package manager and performs no dependency resolution or system integration.

questions.q: You start the Apache web server with 'systemctl start apache2'. After a system reboot, Apache is not running. What additional command ensures Apache starts automatically on every boot?
questions.note: systemctl start runs the service now; systemctl enable creates the symlink that causes it to start at boot. Both commands are typically needed together: start (now) + enable (persistent).

explain.correct: systemctl enable apache2 creates a symbolic link in the appropriate systemd wants directory, causing the service to be started automatically every time the system boots.
wrong: systemctl restart stops and immediately restarts the service but does not configure it to start at boot — it has the same persistence problem.
systemctl reload sends a signal to the running service to re-read its configuration without restarting; it does not affect boot-time behavior.
systemctl status displays the current state and recent log output of the service; it makes no changes to boot configuration.

questions.q: You want to search for the word 'error' (case-insensitive) in all .log files under /var/log/ and suppress any 'Permission denied' messages from appearing on screen. Which command achieves both goals?
questions.note: The -i flag makes grep case-insensitive. Redirecting file descriptor 2 (stderr) to /dev/null discards error messages like 'Permission denied' without affecting stdout output.

explain.correct: grep -i makes the search case-insensitive so 'Error', 'ERROR', and 'error' all match. The 2>/dev/null redirect sends stderr (fd 2) to the null device, silently discarding permission errors while matching lines still print to the terminal.
wrong: grep 'error' /var/log/*.log 2>/dev/null correctly suppresses stderr but the search is case-sensitive — 'Error' or 'ERROR' would not match.
grep -r -i 'error' /var/log/ 1>/dev/null redirects stdout (fd 1) to /dev/null, discarding the matching output you actually want to see, not the error messages.
grep -i 'error' /var/log/*.log | /dev/null attempts to pipe stdout to /dev/null as a file path, which is a syntax error — /dev/null is not a command and the pipe would fail.

questions.q: An administrator needs to add an existing user 'jdoe' to the 'docker' group without removing them from their current groups. Which command accomplishes this correctly?
questions.note: usermod -aG appends (-a) the user to the supplementary group (-G). Omitting -a would replace all supplementary groups, potentially locking the user out of other group-based permissions.

explain.correct: usermod -aG docker jdoe appends jdoe to the docker supplementary group (-G) using the append flag (-a), preserving all existing group memberships. Without -a, -G alone would replace all supplementary groups.
wrong: usermod -g docker jdoe changes jdoe's primary group to docker — it does not add docker as a supplementary group and does not preserve the existing primary group.
groupadd creates a new group; it does not add users to an existing group. The syntax 'groupadd docker jdoe' is invalid.
chown jdoe:docker /etc/group attempts to change the ownership of the /etc/group system file, which is both incorrect and dangerous — it does not modify group membership.

questions.q: The /usr/bin/passwd binary has permissions -rwsr-xr-x and is owned by root. What does the 's' in the owner execute position indicate, and why is it necessary?
options: It is the sticky bit; it keeps the passwd binary in memory for faster execution.
It is the SGID bit; it runs passwd with the privileges of the file's group owner.
It is the SUID bit; it runs passwd with the privileges of the file's owner (root), allowing any user to update /etc/shadow.
It is an immutable flag; it prevents passwd from being modified or deleted.
questions.note: The SUID bit (octal 4xxx) on an executable causes it to run as the file's owner rather than the invoking user. passwd needs root privileges to write to /etc/shadow, which is readable only by root.

explain.correct: The 's' in the owner's execute position is the SUID (Set User ID) bit. When any user runs /usr/bin/passwd, the process temporarily gains root's effective UID, which is required to write the new password hash to /etc/shadow — a file owned by root with mode 640 or 000.
wrong: The sticky bit (octal 1xxx) appears as 't' or 'T' in the other-execute position, not in the owner-execute position. It restricts deletion of files in shared directories like /tmp, and has no effect on memory caching.
The SGID bit appears as 's' in the group-execute position (the middle triplet), not in the owner-execute position. passwd requires the file owner's (root's) privileges, not the group's.
There is no POSIX 'immutable flag' encoded in the standard rwx permission string. Immutability is set via chattr +i and visible with lsattr, not in the ls -l permission field.

questions.q: An administrator creates a new logical volume, formats it as XFS, and mounts it. Six months later, the volume runs low on space. Which of the following statements about managing this XFS volume is TRUE?
options: XFS volumes can be grown and shrunk online using xfs_growfs and xfs_shrink respectively.
XFS volumes can be grown online with xfs_growfs after extending the LV, but XFS cannot be shrunk — a rebuild is required to reduce the filesystem size.
XFS volumes must be unmounted before growing with resize2fs, similar to ext4.
XFS and ext4 both support online shrinking; only btrfs requires an offline operation.
questions.note: XFS supports online growth via xfs_growfs but does NOT support shrinking under any circumstances. This is a critical distinction from btrfs and a common exam trap in CompTIA Linux+ objectives.

explain.correct: XFS is a grow-only filesystem. After using lvextend to expand the logical volume, xfs_growfs can grow the filesystem online while it is mounted. There is no xfs_shrink command; to reduce an XFS filesystem you must back up the data, destroy the filesystem, re-create it smaller, and restore.
wrong: No 'xfs_shrink' command exists. XFS fundamentally cannot be shrunk — this is an architectural limitation of XFS, not a missing tool.
resize2fs is the resize tool for ext2/ext3/ext4 filesystems, not XFS. XFS uses xfs_growfs. Additionally, xfs_growfs can operate on a live, mounted filesystem.
XFS does NOT support online or offline shrinking. ext4 supports offline shrinking via resize2fs. btrfs supports both online grow and online shrink. The statement is factually incorrect on all counts.

questions.q: A sysadmin configures SSH key-based authentication on a Linux server. After copying their public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, login still fails with 'Permission denied (publickey)'. The sysadmin checks and finds ~/.ssh is mode 755 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is mode 644. What is the MOST LIKELY cause?
options: The public key file should be named id_rsa.pub inside ~/.ssh/, not authorized_keys.
SSH requires ~/.ssh to be mode 700 (owner-only) and authorized_keys to be mode 600 (owner-only); the current world-readable permissions cause sshd to reject the file as insecure.
SELinux is blocking the SSH daemon from reading authorized_keys; run 'setenforce 0' to confirm and then permanently set SELinux to permissive mode.
The sshd_config setting 'PubkeyAuthentication yes' must be uncommented and the service restarted before key-based logins work.
questions.note: sshd enforces strict permission checks on ~/.ssh (must be 700) and authorized_keys (must be 600 or 640). If other users can read these files, sshd refuses to use them as a security safeguard. This is one of the most common SSH hardening gotchas.

explain.correct: sshd deliberately rejects authorized_keys if the ~/.ssh directory or the file itself is group- or world-readable/writable. The required permissions are ~/.ssh 700 (drwx------) and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 600 (-rw-------). The fix is: chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
wrong: The authorized_keys file is the correct filename for storing multiple authorized public keys. The private key on the client side is id_rsa (or id_ed25519); the server reads authorized_keys, not id_rsa.pub directly.

While SELinux can interfere with SSH in some contexts, the symptom described — wrong file permissions — is the most likely and direct cause. Setting SELinux to permissive permanently is bad security practice and should never be the first or permanent response. Fix permissions first; investigate SELinux context (restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh) only if permissions are already correct.

PubkeyAuthentication defaults to 'yes' in modern OpenSSH; it is enabled without editing sshd_config. The failure described is a permissions rejection, not a configuration rejection, and sshd would log a different error for a disabled PubkeyAuthentication setting.
